{"result":"# Rust and the Promise of Memory Safety

Rust is a general-purpose programming language that emphasizes performance, type safety, concurrency, and memory safety [1]. Its central promise is memory safety without a garbage collector [2].

Memory safety means being protected from software bugs and security vulnerabilities in memory access, such as buffer overflows and dangling pointers [3]. Java achieves this through runtime checks of array bounds and pointer dereferences [3]. C, C++, and Fortran allow arbitrary pointer arithmetic without bounds checking, which makes them memory-unsafe [3].

Rust's development began when Graydon Hoare started it in 2006, and Mozilla Research sponsored it from 2009 [2]. Although Rust is syntactically similar to C++ [2], it replaces classes and inheritance with structs, enums, traits, and methods [1]. It also draws on functional programming ideas such as immutability and pattern matching [1].
